newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Economists hail Yeltsin talk, restructuring hopes.
newsitem.headline: Economists hail Yeltsin talk, restructuring hopes.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin's forceful state of the nation speech raises hopes that needed restructuring of government and enterprises will now be tackled, but it is uncertain if he can answer the painful questions he raised, economists said.
For many investors the fact that a fit Yeltsin seemed to be in control again on Thursday was the most encouraging event of the day.
"President Yeltsin didn't look like a man who had just had multiple heart surgery. He looked like a man in charge," said Renaissance Capital economist Roland Nash.
Dollar-denominated MinFin bonds, often susceptible to political events, ended up to 110 basis points higher with the market impressed by Yeltsin's performance.
Yeltsin spoke frankly about the problems facing Russian society and the economy, and promised a shake-up of government and rigorous enforcement of the law to put things right.
The address contained few specific policy measures, however. "He gave a lot of questions but there weren't any answers," Nash said.
But Yeltsin did allow himself a few hostages to fortune, setting the government deadlines for a number of reforms.

These ranged from submitting the remainder of a new Tax Code to parliament by the end of the month, to eliminating the primary deficit -- that is balancing the budget except for interest payments on government debt -- by 1999.
United City Bank economist Christopher Granville said the deadlines would make it easier to monitor government performance.
Limiting the time left for the administration to work on the tax code before it goes to parliament would remove the scope for lobbyists to fight for the preservation of tax privileges.
Plans to eliminate the deficit in two years may not be realistic, but at least they show the government does not intend to borrow its way into unsustainable growth, Granville said.
"That doesn't need to be taken literally any more than you would when a U.S. president says the same, but it's an important policy statement," he said.
Yeltsin said tax reform was one of the most important tasks for 1997, and a more equitable tax system would pave the way for investment and economic recovery.
Tax evasion has been a big factor in the revenue shortfalls that have crippled the government, preventing it from paying many salaries, and vexing the International Monetary Fund.

Yeltsin condemned the government for failing to pay wages, which has led to widespread public anger, and promised a radical overhaul of the government, involving changes to both its structure and composition.
A reshuffle in the next few days is likely to bring Yeltsin's chief-of-staff Anatoly Chubais into the cabinet with a top post overseeing the economy, official sources said.

Foreign investors are likely to welcome the return of the ruthlessly efficient but unpopular Chubais, who masterminded Russia's massive privatisation programme until Yeltsin dropped him from the cabinet before last year's presidential election.

But his transfer could initially unsettle some investors who are used to the status quo. They could see his move from heading Yeltsin's administration to a position formally subordinate to Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin as a demotion, Nash said.
Restructuring of the government could be just as important as new faces.

Chernomyrdin promised to upgrade the Economy Ministry into the main economic-policy centre and abolish many Soviet-era branch ministries responsible for individual industrial sectors, which were irrelevant now their industries have been privatised.
Slimming down the bureaucracy in this way has long been urged by reformers.

But it would also remove an important group of lobbyists, as the conservative branch ministries typically see themselves as advocates for "their" industries, intervening when their companies are under pressure to pay tax arrears, for instance.

Yeltsin demonstrated his determination to take on these lobbies by singling out Russia's powerful natural monopolies, such as gas company Gazprom and electricity generator and distributor UES, saying their prices were too high.
Restructuring such enterprises will be the next, and harder, stage of economic reform, now that inflation has been brought down and the economy stabilised, Granville said.
